title: Boom, Buzz, Whisper
subtitle: What sound is and how you hear it
subject: Physics

p: Every sound is a wobble. A drum skin wobbles up and down. A guitar string wobbles back and forth. The wobble bumps the air. The air bumps more air. The bumps race out in all directions, like ripples in a pond. When they reach your ear, you hear.
pages.cap: The speaker wobbles. The air wobbles. Your ear catches it.
pages.fact: Did you know? You cannot see sound waves, but you can feel them if you stand near a big speaker.

p: Put your fingers on your throat. Now hum. Feel that buzz? That is your voice. Two little flaps in your throat wobble when air passes. Hum low and they wobble slowly. Hum high and they wobble fast. Every word you say starts as a wobble.
pages.cap: Your throat buzzes when you hum. That buzz is sound being made.

pages.h: Sound needs something to travel through
p: Sound travels through air. It travels through water too. Whales call to each other under the sea. It even travels through walls and wood. Press your ear on a table and tap the other end. The tap sounds loud and close. Solid things carry sound very well.
pages.cap: Sound can travel through gas, liquid and solid things.

opts: A wobble that moves through the air
pages.why: Sound is a wobble, or vibration, that travels through air, water or solid things.

pages.h: In space, nobody can hear a rocket
p: Space is empty. There is no air to wobble. A rocket could roar right past you and you would hear nothing. Astronauts talk by radio instead.

Sound is fast, but light is much faster. In a storm, you see the flash first. The boom comes later. Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 kilometre. Count the seconds between flash and boom. Divide by three. That is how many kilometres away the storm is.
pages.cap: Flash now, boom later. Light wins the race every time.
pages.fact: Did you know? Sound moves about 340 metres every second. A jet plane can go faster than that!

p: A big wobble makes a loud sound. A small wobble makes a quiet one. We measure loudness in decibels. A whisper is about 30. Talking is about 60. A lawnmower is about 90. A rock concert is about 110. A jet taking off is about 140. Ouch!
pages.cap: Each bar shows how loud a sound is.

p: Your ears are soft inside. Very loud sounds can hurt them. Sounds over 85 decibels, for a long time, can wear your hearing down. It does not grow back. So cover your ears near fireworks. Turn headphones down. If you have to shout to be heard, it is too loud.
pages.cap: Cover your ears when a sound is too loud. Your ears will thank you.

p: A fast wobble makes a high sound, like a bird's tweet. A slow wobble makes a low sound, like a big drum. Small things wobble fast. Big things wobble slowly. That is why a tiny bell rings high and a long, thick string hums low.
pages.cap: A short pendulum swings fast. Fast wobbles make high sounds.

p: A bee does not sing. Its wings make the buzz. They flap about 200 times every second! That fast flapping wobbles the air. A mosquito flaps even faster, so its whine is higher. A big bumblebee flaps slower, so its buzz is lower.
pages.cap: Buzz! The bee's wings beat the air 200 times a second.

pages.why: Fast wobbles make high sounds. Slow wobbles make low sounds.

p: Your ear is shaped like a cup to catch sound. The sound goes down a tunnel. At the end is a thin skin called the eardrum. The wobbling air makes the eardrum wobble too. Deeper inside, a tiny snail-shaped part turns the wobble into a message for your brain.
pages.cap: Sound enters the ear and makes the eardrum wobble.

p: Behind your eardrum are the three smallest bones in your body. The littlest one is about 3 millimetres long. That is smaller than a grain of rice. They are fully grown when you are born. They pass the wobble along, from the eardrum to the snail-shaped part.
pages.cap: The three smallest bones in your body are inside your ear.
pages.fact: Did you know? The three ear bones are called the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup.

p: Shout in a big empty room or near a cliff. Your shout comes back! Sound bounces off hard walls like a ball. The bounce is called an echo. Soft things like curtains and carpets soak sound up. That is why a room with no furniture sounds so loud.
pages.cap: Sound hits the wall and bounces back to you.

p: A bat hunts at night. It is dark. So the bat shouts tiny squeaks, too high for you to hear. The squeaks bounce off a moth and come back. The bat hears the echo and knows where the moth is. Dolphins do the same trick under water.
pages.cap: The bat's squeak bounces off the moth. The echo tells it where to fly.

p: Send your voice down a string.
steps: Poke a small hole in the bottom of two paper cups.
Push a long piece of string through both holes. Tie a knot in each end.
Walk apart until the string is tight.
Whisper into one cup. Your friend listens at the other!
pages.cap: Your voice wobbles the cup, the string and the other cup.
pages.safe: Ask a grown-up to poke the holes.

p: Sound moves through water four times faster than through air. The sea is full of sounds. Shrimp snap. Fish grunt. Whales sing. A blue whale makes one of the loudest calls of any animal. Other whales can hear it hundreds of kilometres away.
pages.cap: Deep in the dark sea, animals find each other by sound.

p: Some sounds are too high for people to hear. A dog can hear them. That is how a dog whistle works. Some sounds are too low. Elephants rumble so low you cannot hear it. But other elephants can, from many kilometres away. The air is full of secret sounds.
pages.cap: Many animals hear sounds that we never notice.

pages.q: How does a bat find a moth in the dark?
opts: It listens for echoes of its squeaks
pages.why: The bat's squeaks bounce off the moth. The echo tells the bat where it is.

p: In 1883, a volcano called Krakatoa blew up. It made the loudest sound people have ever recorded. The bang was heard almost 5,000 kilometres away. That is farther than from Toronto all the way to Vancouver. The air wobble went around the whole Earth.
pages.cap: The Krakatoa volcano made a bang heard on the other side of the ocean.

p: Every instrument makes a wobble. A guitar wobbles a string. A drum wobbles a skin. A flute wobbles the air inside a tube. Your voice wobbles two flaps in your throat. Short strings and short tubes make high notes. Long ones make low notes.
pages.cap: Strings, skins and tubes all wobble to make music.

p: Scientists built a room with thick, soft walls. The walls soak up every sound. Nothing echoes. It is the quietest room on Earth. Stand inside it, and you hear your own heartbeat. You hear your blood moving. Some people cannot stay in there for long.
pages.cap: In a very quiet room you can hear your own heart beating.

pages.h: A whale's song can cross an ocean
p: Humpback whales sing long songs that last for hours. In the deep sea, the sound rolls on and on. Other whales far, far away stop to listen.
Make sound jump.
steps: Stretch plastic wrap tight over a bowl.
Sprinkle a few grains of rice on top.
Hold a metal pot near the bowl and bang it with a spoon.
Watch the rice jump! The sound wobbled the plastic.
pages.cap: The sound from the pot wobbles the plastic and makes the rice dance.
